doc.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 25, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Music as uplift: Montgomery bus boycott songs and the artist's duty
summary: He ties music to hope, describes King's songs during the boycott, and a Pittsburgh donor's peak experiences, urging artists to lead out of Covid.

story.theme_name: Late-career reflections: awards, legacy and life lessons
story.community_name: Life philosophy: faith, karma and how to live

blocks.x: Okay. Well it’s a little ironic, I was thinking about last November for some reason was a particularly bad month for me and my cohorts gig-wise. And now those are the good old days.

Oh gosh. Yeah. You know it’s up to, the hardest part about being an artist or a musician I think is the creation, the continuous creation of art and we have to look at this time as that’s another part of the gift, to get ourselves physically together, that’s why I try to walk as much as I can every day. We’ve been doing about two miles a day. Not a lot and I should do more. You know and try to eat right. But then getting down into making yourself better as an artist — all that stuff that you want to give to people, that you know that our job is to lift them up. That there is hope in the darkness. And we can provide that hope through the music, because music can lift people. And that’s why, during, we’ve talked a lot about civil rights and protesting, during the Civil Rights Era it was the music that made people get up and march. And so during the Montgomery bus boycott one of the things Martin Luther King did during that period of time is he said before I speak, and sometimes they would have church every night because he knew that would energize people, right? And imagine like going, deciding I’m not going to go on the bus, but that means I have to walk an hour to work. And so King said before I even speak — when we have church every night before I even speak we’re going to sing for like twenty minutes. You know what they sang? “Nobody Knows the Trouble I’ve Seen.” But they also sang “I’m Gonna Move On Up a Little Higher.” They also sang, “I Ain’t Gonna Let Nobody Turn Me Round.” And then they sang “I’ve been ‘buked and I’ve been scorned/I’ve been

talked about sho’s you’re born.” But then they’d say, “I’m going to ride that glory train/the only way for me to get to heaven is to ride that glory train.” And they would clap their hands and there was the physiology about the movement and the physical act of singing that brings joy. And that’s what I’m charged to do, what we’re charged to do as musicians, is to bring that joy in the sense of music. And it can be non, even non-verbal is better. I was working with the Pittsburgh Symphony recently and some of their donors and just having a conversation with them and I asked one of the guys I said, “What’s one of your best musical experiences.” And he said, “You know I’m a very religious man,” he says, “but I have to tell you the best experiences, the peak experiences that I’ve had in my life have been in the concert hall watching the Pittsburgh Symphony, not necessarily having, you know what I’m saying? So this is the power of music and I think we have to hone our focus on that and as Bernstein said play more devotedly and perform even harder than we ever have before, to squeeze the juice out of the joy and the majesty of great jazz and great music. And that’s the thing. Because the artists can lead where we’re going in this revolution, getting out of Covid. We have to lead it.
